summary.text:
Working in the \(p\)-adics, the proof splits the summation into \(p\mid k\) and \(p
mid k\), using \( inom{pM+k}{k}= inom{M+\lfloor k/pfloor}{\lfloor k/pfloor}\prod_{p
mid i\le k}(1+pM/i)\). For the first part, a second-order expansion of this product together with Wolstenholme-type bounds on the reciprocal and reciprocal-square sums gives three powers of \(p\); for the second, regrouping reduced residues into \(p\)-blocks yields a descent estimate for an auxiliary binomial sum, and extracting the full \(p\)-power from \(n\) reduces the general case to \(p
mid n\).

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(m)=\frac1m\sum_{k=0}^m (m+2k)\binom{m+k-1}{k}^{3}\qquad(m\geq 1).
\]
We prove that, for every prime \(p\geq5\) and positive integers \(n,r\),
\[
a(np^r)\equiv a(np^{r-1})\pmod {p^{3r}}.
\]

Throughout the main part of the proof, work in the field \(\mathbf Q_p\), write \(|\cdot|\) for its normalized absolute value, and put \(q=p^{-1}\). Thus \(|p|=q\), every integer has absolute value at most \(1\), and, for an integer \(z\),
\[
 |z|\le q^e\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad p^e\mid z.
\]
We repeatedly use the ultrametric inequality
\[
\left|\sum_i x_i\right|\leq \max_i|x_i|.
\]
Since \(p\ge5\), both \(2\) and \(3\) are \(p\)-adic units.

We first establish the auxiliary estimates needed later.

### 1. Products and a binomial-product splitting

If \(|x_i|\leq\delta\leq1\), then induction on the number of factors, using the ultrametric inequality, gives
\[
 \left|\prod_i(1+x_i)-1\right|\leq\delta,
 \qquad
 \left|\prod_i(1+x_i)\right|\leq1.
\]
A second-order version, also obtained by induction, is
\[
\left|\prod_i(1+x_i)-
\left(1+S+\frac{S^2-Q}{2}\right)\right|\leq\delta^3,
\tag{1}
\]
where \(S=\sum_i x_i\) and \(Q=\sum_i x_i^2\). Indeed, on adjoining a new variable \(x\), the difference between the two sides’ approximating polynomials changes by
\[
 (1+x)\left(P-1-S-\frac{S^2-Q}{2}\right)
 +x\frac{S^2-Q}{2}.
\]
The first summand has norm at most \(\delta^3\), while
\(|S|\leq\delta\), \(|Q|\leq\delta^2\), and hence the second does too. Division by \(2\) does not change norms.

We will also use
\[
 |X^3-1|\leq |X-1|\quad\text{if }|X|\leq1,
\tag{2}
\]
because \(X^3-1=(X-1)(X^2+X+1)\) and the second factor has norm at most \(1\).

For \(N,k\geq0\), define
\[
 I_p(k)=\{i:1\leq i\leq k,\ p\nmid i\},
 \qquad
 E(N,k)=\prod_{i\in I_p(k)}\left(1+\frac Ni\right).
\]
If \(N=pM\), then
\[
 \binom{N+k}{k}=\binom{M+\lfloor k/p\rfloor}{\lfloor k/p\rfloor}E(N,k).
\tag{3}
\]
To see this, write
\[
 \binom{N+k}{k}=\prod_{i=1}^k\frac{N+i}{i}

after embedding in \(\mathbf Q_p\). Separate the factors with \(p\mid i\). Writing \(i=pt\), such a factor becomes
\[
 \frac{pM+pt}{pt}=\frac{M+t}{t},
\]
and their product is the smaller binomial coefficient in (3). The remaining factors form \(E(N,k)\).

Every denominator in \(E(N,k)\) is a unit, so
\[
 |E(N,k)-1|\leq |N|,
 \qquad |E(N,k)|\leq1,
 \qquad |E(N,k)^3-1|\leq |N|.
\tag{4}
\]

### 2. Wolstenholme-type reciprocal-sum estimates

For \(\beta\geq1\), let
\[
 R_\beta=\{u:0\leq u<p^\beta,\ p\nmid u\}

a
\]
and define
\[
 G_\beta(w)=\sum_{u\in R_\beta}\frac1{(u+p^\beta w)^2}.
\]
(The displayed stray “a” should be ignored: the definition is simply the set and sum shown.) We claim
\[
 |G_\beta(w)|\leq q^\beta\qquad(\beta\geq1,w\geq0).
\tag{5}
\]

First consider
\[
 T_\beta=\sum_{u\in R_\beta}\frac1{u^2}.
\]
Put \(Q=p^\beta\). Since \(Q\) is odd, \(c=(Q+1)/2\) is an inverse of \(2\) modulo \(Q\). Thus multiplication by \(2\) modulo \(Q\),
\(c3(u)=2u\bmod Q\), permutes \(R_\beta\), with inverse multiplication by \(c\). For each \(u\in R_\beta\), the integers \(\sigma(u)\) and \(2u\) differ by a multiple of \(Q\). Both are \(p\)-adic units, and the identity
\[
 \frac1{x^2}-\frac1{y^2}=\frac{(y-x)(y+x)}{x^2y^2}
\]
therefore gives
\[
 \left|\frac1{\sigma(u)^2}-\frac1{(2u)^2}\right|\leq q^\beta.
\]
Summing and reindexing by the permutation \(\sigma\),
\[
 \left|T_\beta-\frac14T_\beta\right|\leq q^\beta.
\]
But \(1-1/4=3/4\) is a \(p\)-adic unit because \(p\geq5\). Hence
\[
 |T_\beta|\leq q^\beta.
\tag{6}
\]
For each \(u\in R_\beta\), the two units \(u+p^\beta w\) and \(u\) differ by a multiple of \(p^\beta\), so the same inverse-square identity shows that their reciprocal squares differ by something of norm at most \(q^\beta\). Combining this with (6) proves (5).

We next need sums over a longer interval. For \(B=b p^\beta\), decomposition into blocks
\[
 i=u+p^\beta w,\qquad 0\leq w<b,\quad u\in R_\beta,
\]
is a bijection from the integers \(1\leq i\leq B\) not divisible by \(p\) to these pairs. Consequently (5) gives
\[
 \left|\sum_{i\in I_p(B)}\frac1{i^2}\right|\leq q^\beta.
\tag{7}
\]
There is also the stronger first-reciprocal estimate
\[
 \left|\sum_{i\in I_p(B)}\frac1i\right|\leq q^{2\beta}.
\tag{8}
\]
Indeed, \(i\mapsto B-i\) permutes \(I_p(B)\): the possible endpoint \(i=B\) is absent because \(p\mid B\). Pairing a sum with its reflected copy yields
\[
 2\sum_{i\in I_p(B)}\frac1i
 =B\sum_{i\in I_p(B)}\frac1{i(B-i)}.
\tag{9}
\]
Now
\[
 \frac1{i(B-i)}+\frac1{i^2}
 =\frac{B}{i^2(B-i)}.
\]
All denominators here are units, so each term on the right has norm at most \(|B|\leq q^\beta\). By (7), the sum in the right side of (9) has norm at most \(q^\beta\). Since also \(|B|\leq q^\beta\) and \(|2|=1\), (8) follows.

### 3. A refined estimate for \(E(N,k)-1\)

Suppose
\[
 |N|\leq q^{\rho+1},\qquad j=j''p^u,\qquad p\nmid j''.

a
\]
Then
\[
 \left|E(N,pj)-1\right|
 \leq q^{3+\min\{\rho+2u,\,2\rho+u,\,3\rho\}}.
\tag{10}
\]
Again, the stray “a” in the display has no mathematical content.

To prove (10), apply (1) to \(x_i=N/i\), with \(i\in I_p(pj)\) and \(\delta=q^{\rho+1}\). Put
\[
 S_1=\sum_{i\in I_p(pj)}\frac1i,
 \qquad S_2=\sum_{i\in I_p(pj)}\frac1{i^2}.
\]
Since \(pj=j''p^{u+1}\), (7) and (8), with \(\beta=u+1\), give
\[
 |S_1|\leq q^{2(u+1)},\qquad |S_2|\leq q^{u+1}.
\]
In (1), the linear and quadratic sums are
\[
 S=NS_1,
 \qquad Q=N^2S_2.
\]
Hence
\[
 |S|\leq q^{3+\rho+2u},
 \qquad |Q|\leq q^{3+2\rho+u}.
\]
Also \(|S^2|\leq q^{3+\rho+2u}\), because \(|S|\leq1\), and the remainder in (1) is bounded by
\[
 \delta^3=q^{3\rho+3}.
\]
The ultrametric inequality applied to
\[
 E(N,pj)-1=
 \left(E(N,pj)-1-S-\frac{S^2-Q}{2}\right)
 +S+\frac{S^2-Q}{2}
\]
now proves (10). By (2), the same right side bounds \(|E(N,pj)^3-1|\).

### 4. A descent estimate

Define
\[
 X(m,\beta)=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}\binom{m+j}{j}^3G_\beta(m+j).
\]
By (5) and integrality of the binomial coefficients,
\[
 |X(m,\beta)|\leq q^\beta.
\tag{11}
\]
The shifted reciprocal sums satisfy the exact block identity
\[
 \sum_{t=0}^{p-1}G_\beta(pW+t)=G_{\beta+1}(W).
\tag{12}
\]
Indeed, writing an element of \(R_{\beta+1}\) uniquely as
\(u+p^\beta t\), with \(u\in R_\beta\) and \(0\leq t<p\), transforms the left side term by term into the right side.

Split the index in \(X(pm,\beta)\) as \(j=p\ell+t\), where
\(0\leq\ell<m\) and \(0\leq t<p\). Formula (3) gives
\[
 \binom{pm+p\ell+t}{p\ell+t}
 =\binom{m+\ell}{\ell}E(pm,p\ell+t).
\]
If the factor \(E^3\) is replaced by \(1\), then summing over \(t\) and using (12) gives exactly \(X(m,\beta+1)\). The error in every term is bounded, by (4) and (5), by
\[
 |pm|q^\beta,
\]
while the binomial factor has norm at most \(1\). Thus
\[
 |X(pm,\beta)-X(m,\beta+1)|\leq |pm|q^\beta.
\tag{13}
\]

Suppose now that \(p\nmid n\). Iterating (13), with (11) as the initial case, gives
\[
 |X(np^b,\beta)|\leq q^{b+\beta}\qquad(b\geq0,\ \beta\geq1).
\tag{14}
\]
For completeness, the induction step writes
\[
 X(np^{b+1},\beta)
 =\bigl(X(p(np^b),\beta)-X(np^b,\beta+1)\bigr)
  +X(np^b,\beta+1).
\]
The first term is at most \(|np^{b+1}|q^\beta=q^{b+1+\beta}\), and the induction hypothesis gives the same bound for the second.

### 5. The sum over indices not divisible by \(p\)

For the moment assume \(p\nmid n\), let \(r\geq1\), and put
\[
 N=np^r,\qquad M=np^{r-1},
\]
so \(N=pM\). Define the summand
\[
 F_N(k)=\frac{N+2k}{N}\binom{N+k-1}{k}^3.
\]
We prove
\[
 \left|\sum_{\substack{0\leq k\leq N\\p\nmid k}}F_N(k)\right|
 \leq q^{3r}.
\tag{15}
\]

Every relevant \(k\) has a unique expression
\[
 k=pj+s,\qquad 0\leq j<M,\quad 0<s<p.
\]
Equivalently, \(s\in R_1\). Since \(p\nmid k\) and \(p\mid N\), both \(k\) and \(N+k\) are units. The elementary identity
\[
 \binom{N+k-1}{k}(N+k)=N\binom{N+k}{k},

together with (3), gives
\[
 F_N(k)=
 \frac{(N+2k)N^2}{(N+k)^3} inom{M+j}{j}^3E(N,k)^3.
\tag{16}
\]
Compare this with
\[
 \frac{2N^2}{(N+k)^2}\binom{M+j}{j}^3.
\]
Using \(N+2k=2(N+k)-N\), subtraction yields exactly
\[
 \frac{(N+2k)N^2}{(N+k)^3}\binom{M+j}{j}^3(E(N,k)^3-1)
 -\frac{N^3}{(N+k)^3}\binom{M+j}{j}^3.
\tag{17}
\]
Now \(|N|=q^r\), \(|N+k|=1\), the binomial coefficient has norm at most \(1\), and (4) gives \(|E^3-1|\leq|N|\). Each term in (17) therefore has norm at most \(q^{3r}\).

On summing the comparison terms over \((j,s)\), their total is
\[
 2N^2X(M,1),
\]
because the inner sum over \(s\in R_1\) is precisely \(G_1(M+j)\). By (14),
\[
 |X(M,1)|=|X(np^{r-1},1)|\leq q^r.
\]
Thus \(|2N^2X(M,1)|\leq q^{3r}\). The termwise errors (17) also have total norm at most \(q^{3r}\), proving (15).

### 6. The terms whose indices are divisible by \(p\)

We next prove
\[
 \left|\sum_{j=0}^{M} igl(F_{pM}(pj)-F_M(j)\bigr)\right|
 \leq q^{3r},
\qquad M=np^{r-1}.
\tag{18}
\]
The term \(j=0\) is zero, because both summands equal \(1\). Consider \(j\geq1\). From
\[
 \binom{A+k-1}{k}=\frac{A}{A+k}\binom{A+k}{k}
\]
and (3), direct cancellation gives
\[
 F_{pM}(pj)-F_M(j)
 =\frac{(M+2j)M^2}{(M+j)^3} inom{M+j}{j}^3
   \bigl(E(pM,pj)^3-1\bigr).
\tag{19}
\]
We show that every expression in (19) has norm at most
\(q^{3+3\rho}\), where \(\rho=r-1\); this is \(q^{3r}\).

Write
\[
 M=np^\rho,
 \qquad j=j''p^u,
 \qquad p\nmid j''.
\]
Then
\[
 |M|=q^\rho,\qquad |j|=|2j|=q^u.
\]
By (10), applied to \(N=pM\),
\[
 |E(pM,pj)^3-1|
 \leq q^{3+\min\{\rho+2u,\,2\rho+u,\,3\rho\}}.
\tag{20}
\]
We distinguish three cases.

* If \(u<\rho\), the unequal-norm rule in a nonarchimedean field gives
\[
 |M+j|=|M+2j|=q^u,
\]
and the minimum in (20) is \(\rho+2u\). Bounding the binomial coefficient by \(1\), the norm of (19) is at most
\[
 \frac{q^u q^{2\rho}q^{3+\rho+2u}}{q^{3u}}
 =q^{3+3\rho}.
\]

* If \(u>\rho\), then
\[
 |M+j|=|M+2j|=q^\rho,
\]
and the minimum in (20) is \(3\rho\). Thus the bound is
\[
 \frac{q^\rho q^{2\rho}q^{3+3\rho}}{q^{3\rho}}
 =q^{3+3\rho}.
\]

* Suppose \(u=\rho\). Cancellation could make \(|M+j|\) smaller, so a crude unit bound for the binomial coefficient is insufficient. Use
\[
 (M+j)\binom{M+j-1}{j-1}=j\binom{M+j}{j}.
\]
The first binomial coefficient is integral, hence
\[
 \left|\binom{M+j}{j}\right|\,|j|\leq |M+j|.
\]
Writing \(\tau=|M+j|\), this says
\[
 \left|\binom{M+j}{j}\right|\leq \tau/q^\rho.
\]
Also \(|M+2j|\leq q^\rho\), and (20) again has exponent \(3+3\rho\). Therefore the norm of (19) is at most
\[
 \frac{q^\rho q^{2\rho}(\tau/q^\rho)^3q^{3+3\rho}}{\tau^3}
 =q^{3+3\rho}.
\]

This proves the desired termwise estimate in all cases. The ultrametric inequality, together with the zero term at \(j=0\), proves (18).

### 7. Integrality and assembly when \(p\nmid n\)

We must justify that the defining quotient is an integer and that it can be represented by the displayed \(p\)-adic sum. Let
\[
 S_m=\sum_{k=0}^m(m+2k)\binom{m+k-1}{k}^3.
\]
The following identity proves \(m\mid S_m\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
S_m=m\Bigg(&\sum_{k=0}^m
 \binom{m+k}{k}\binom{m+k-1}{k}^2\\
&+\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}
 \binom{m+k}{k}\binom{m+k}{k+1}^2\Bigg).
\tag{21}
\end{aligned}
\]
To verify it, split \(m+2k=(m+k)+k\). In the first resulting sum use
\[
 (m+k)\binom{m+k-1}{k}=m\binom{m+k}{k}.
\]
In the second, shift \(k\) to \(k+1\) and use
\[
 (k+1)\binom{m+k}{k+1}=m\binom{m+k}{k}.
\]
This gives (21). Also symmetry gives
\( inom{m+k-1}{m-1}=\binom{m+k-1}{k}\), so (21) applies exactly to the sequence in the question. Consequently, in \(\mathbf Q_p\),
\[
 a(m)=\sum_{k=0}^m\frac{m+2k}{m}\binom{m+k-1}{k}^3.
\tag{22}
\]

Apply (22) with \(N=np^r\) and \(M=np^{r-1}\). Split the sum for \(a(N)\) into indices divisible by \(p\) and indices not divisible by \(p\). The divisible indices are exactly \(k=pj\), \(0\leq j\leq M\). Therefore
\[
 a(N)-a(M)
 =\sum_{j=0}^M\bigl(F_N(pj)-F_M(j)\bigr)
  +\sum_{\substack{0\leq k\leq N\\p\nmid k}}F_N(k).
\]
The first sum has norm at most \(q^{3r}\) by (18), and the second by (15). Hence
\[
 |a(np^r)-a(np^{r-1})|\leq q^{3r}.
\]
Both quantities are integers, so the norm-divisibility criterion gives
\[
 p^{3r}\mid a(np^r)-a(np^{r-1}).
\tag{23}
\]
This proves the theorem under the temporary assumption \(p\nmid n\).

### 8. Removal of the condition \(p\nmid n\)

For arbitrary positive \(n\), write
\[
 n=n'p^s,
 \qquad p\nmid n'.
\]
Applying (23) to \(n'\) and exponent \(r+s\) yields
\[
 a(n'p^{r+s})\equiv a(n'p^{r+s-1})
 \pmod {p^{3(r+s)}}.
\]
Since \(r>0\),
\[
 n'p^{r+s}=np^r,
 \qquad n'p^{r+s-1}=np^{r-1}.
\]
Finally, \(p^{3r}\mid p^{3(r+s)}\), so reducing the modulus gives
\[
 \boxed{a(np^r)\equiv a(np^{r-1})\pmod {p^{3r}}}.
\]
This holds for every prime \(p\geq5\) and all positive integers \(n,r\), as required.
